principles.text: Never judge market health from a single index indicator (e.g. QQQ below the 20 EMA); analyze the action of individual stocks first - if leaders are finding support at rising EMAs and building higher lows, the market is fine regardless of the index chart.

IWM/small-cap relative strength is a better breadth gauge than the cap-weighted indexes; when small caps keep outperforming during a pullback, breadth is improving and the odds of a deep correction are statistically lower.
In a fast 'lockout rally' market, keep making entries on pullback days rather than waiting for the uptrend to be obvious - missing the first day or two of the new leg means being left out entirely.
When buying a pullback, don't buy on the way down - wait for the stock to find the support level and then take the first 5-minute or 15-minute candle breakout as the entry trigger.
After a gap up, the best entry is the intraday dip into the 9/21 EMA or into the newly created gap, rather than chasing the gap open itself.
Avoid wide-spread, thin stocks even when the setup is good - a ~$12 bid-ask spread is reason enough to take the equally good but more liquid alternative.

Define the stop before entry as the level that proves the trade wrong, then trust it - trying to outsmart your stops occasionally helps but loses over time when the market is still range-bound rather than extended.
Non-low-of-day stops (the 5- or 15-minute breakout candle low) lower your win rate but tighten risk substantially; accept the extra stop-outs and be willing to re-enter if the stock bounces back.
Only sell into strength or close positions early when the market is genuinely extended; inside a range/pullback, let the stops do the selling.

To capture big trends you must hold through pullbacks and ugly red days - if you sell your leaders on every red day you exit at a third of the move; if holding everything is too hard, sell some into strength and hold the rest with realized profits as a cushion.

Losing trades are not the same as bad trades - lose small and win big; a triple-digit year is possible while making many mistakes, because the edge comes from continually correcting them, not from IQ.

It's better to miss an opportunity than to chase an extended move and get stopped out - chasing damages mental capital and makes you hesitate on the next valid setup, and a bull market always offers more opportunities.

Don't blindly copy another trader's rules - question each one, adopt only what fits your personality and style, and modify the rest; disagreeing with famous traders after thinking it through is part of improving.
Always study your losing trades; a trader who stops examining mistakes and looking for room to improve is doomed to fail no matter past success.
When traveling, trade less: let stops manage existing positions, take only A+ setups or none at all - trades made while traveling are generally bad.

The best opportunities show up during pullbacks and weakness - at support in an intact uptrend, don't get super bearish or ignore the upside potential, even if this bounce isn't guaranteed to be the next leg up.
